title: The Extinct “American Cheetah” Wasn’t a Cheetah After All - Nautilus
gist: A new Current Biology study finds that the extinct 'American cheetah' (Miracinonyx trumani), which roamed North American grasslands from 2.5 million to 16,000 years ago, was not the specialized cheetah-like sprinter its cheetah-convergent body plan suggested but instead a more flexible carnivore, illustrating how convergent fossil morphology can mislead species classification.

insights.claim: The extinct 'American cheetah' (Miracinonyx trumani), despite having a streamlined body, long legs, and large nostrils resembling an African cheetah built for sprinting after prey, is now understood by a new Current Biology study to not have been a specialized savanna sprinter in the same way as the African cheetah, and per the subheading was instead a more flexible, generalist carnivore.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A textbook case of convergent-evolution misclassification: cheetah-like morphology does not necessarily imply cheetah-like ecology or behavior, a caution relevant to any inference from form to function in comparative biology.

insights.claim: Miracinonyx trumani roamed the open grasslands of North America from about 2.5 million years ago until roughly 16,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: Establishes the timeframe of this Pleistocene megafauna species relevant to paleoecology research.

insights.claim: Study first author Molly Cassatt-Johnstone (UC Santa Cruz graduate student) noted it is very hard to interpret an unseen prehistoric species without comparing it to a known living analog — a methodological bias that likely produced the original 'cheetah' mislabeling.
insights.speaker: Devin Reese
insights.so_what: A general caution for paleobiology and any inference-from-analogy research: absence of a living reference species biases classification toward the nearest known analog.
insights.quote: It's very hard to imagine a prehistoric species we've never seen without comparing it to something we know
